meta.description: An adaptive interactive derivatives course for upper-secondary students
meta.ogDescription: Adaptive exercises with proofs built from limits and difference quotients.

overview.title: Derivatives:
overview.intro: We start with a concrete question—how do you measure velocity at a single instant?—and build the geometry, definition and rules without skipping steps.
overview.question: QUESTION {{number}}
overview.unlock: The answer is revealed after reading “{{section}}”.

geometry.q: How do you find a slope on a curve?
geometry.label: GEOMETRIC
geometry.title: A slope
geometry.answer: It is the slope of the tangent line, obtained as the limit of secant lines.

analytic.label: ANALYTIC
analytic.title: A limit
analytic.answer: It is the limit of the difference quotient as the increment tends to zero without becoming zero.

application.label: APPLIED
application.title: An instantaneous rate
application.answer: It measures how quickly a quantity changes, with a sign and a precise unit.

lesson1.title: The concept of derivative
lesson1.subtitle: From motion to the formal definition
lesson1.objective: Build the derivative as a geometric, analytic and physical object.

lesson2.title: Rules, Taylor and theorems
lesson2.subtitle: From proofs to calculation mastery
lesson2.objective: Derive rules from limits, apply them and explore the main theorems through figures and practical cases.

overview.sourceBody: Browse the project, documentation and change history on GitHub.

velocita.title: Velocity at a single instant
velocita.lead: Before the formula comes the problem: average velocity belongs to a time interval, but how can we express velocity at an instant with no duration?

geometria.title: The secant becomes a tangent
geometria.lead: The derivative arises geometrically by bringing two points on a graph closer. Move h and watch the secant slope converge to the tangent slope.

definizione.title: The formal definition
definizione.lead: We now give precise form to the geometric and physical intuition. The derivative exists when the difference quotient tends to a finite value.

derivabilita.title: Continuous does not mean differentiable
derivabilita.lead: A differentiable function is always continuous. The converse can fail: a graph may be unbroken and still have a corner or vertical tangent.

interpretazioni.title: Three ways to say “derivative”
interpretazioni.lead: The same mathematical object describes a slope, a limit and a rate of change. Moving between these interpretations is the real goal of the lesson.

warmup.title: Three questions to restart
warmup.lead: Before building operational rules, recall the ideas from lesson one. Answer aloud or on paper, then open the correction.

fondamentali.title: Building the table together
fondamentali.lead: The middle column matters most: remember which idea produces each formula, so you can reconstruct it when memory is not enough.

regole.title: Four rules, four ideas
regole.lead: For every rule we connect the working formula, its proof from limits and its verbal reading. A rule is ready to use only after understanding where it comes from.

derivata-seconda.title: The derivative of the derivative
derivata-seconda.lead: f″ measures how slope changes. On a graph it describes concavity; in motion it describes acceleration.

taylor.title: The local DNA of a function
taylor.lead: Taylor answers a concrete question: near a chosen point, can a difficult function be replaced by a simpler polynomial that closely resembles it?

teoremi.title: The theorems that put derivatives to work
teoremi.lead: This is not yet a full function study; it is a toolkit. Every theorem starts from a figure, answers a concrete question and clearly states when it can be used.

differenceQuotient.definition: The ratio between the change in a function and the change h in its variable. The derivative arises from its limit.

secant.definition: A line through two points of a graph. As the points move closer, secants may tend to the tangent.

tangent.definition: A line with the same local direction as the graph at a point; its slope is the derivative.

differentiability.definition: The existence of a finite derivative at a point, with the same limit from the left and right.

prosthaphaeresis.definition: A trigonometric identity that turns sums or differences of sines and cosines into products.

operatorNotation.definition: The notation Df, which treats differentiation as an operation applied to the function f.

curvature.definition: A geometric measure of how quickly a curve changes direction. It adds information beyond the sign of f″.

osculatingCircle.definition: A circle that locally approximates the position, direction and curvature of a curve.

maclaurin.definition: The Taylor polynomial centered at x₀=0, named after Colin Maclaurin.

adequality.definition: A historical method for finding tangents and extrema, developed by Fermat before infinitesimal calculus.

darboux.definition: The theorem stating that a derivative takes every intermediate value even when it is not continuous.

cauchy.definition: The mathematician who made limits, continuity and the generalized mean value theorem rigorous.

conclusionPage.geometry: What can I see on the graph?

intro.paragraph1: A composite function is a function inside another. The value of \(x\) does not reach the sine directly: it is first transformed into \(x^2\), then the result enters the sine. Each transformation is a layer.
intro.paragraph2: Think of an onion: the outer formula wraps the inner ones. To differentiate correctly we remove one layer at a time, skipping none.

buildBox.overline: FIRST: HOW THE FUNCTION IS BUILT
buildBox.title: From the inside out
buildBox.subtitle: Follow the journey of the value of x: the output of one layer becomes the input of the next.
buildBox.ariaLabel: Layered construction of sine of x squared

deriveBox.title: From the outside in
deriveBox.subtitle: Now we reverse the perspective: we start from the last layer applied, the outermost one. After differentiating it, we enter the next layer and multiply the new factor.

derivativeLayers.label: START FROM THE OUTSIDE
derivativeLayers.title: Differentiate the sine, but leave what it contains unchanged
derivativeLayers.explanation: The derivative of sine is cosine. In this first step x² stays inside the parentheses, unchanged: we have not differentiated it yet.

derivativeLayers.label: ENTER THE NEXT LAYER
derivativeLayers.title: Now differentiate the inner part
derivativeLayers.explanation: Once the sine layer is removed, we encounter the elementary function x². Its derivative is 2x.

derivativeLayers.label: LINK THE EFFECTS
derivativeLayers.title: Multiply the derivatives collected along the way
derivativeLayers.explanation: The first factor describes how the sine reacts; the second describes how quickly its input x² changes.

whyMultiply.title: Why do the derivatives multiply?
whyMultiply.paragraph: A small change in \(x\) is first multiplied by the \(x^2\) layer by the factor \(2x\): the absolute value tells how much it changes, the sign also in which direction. That change then reaches the sine and is multiplied again by \(\cos(x^2)\).
whyMultiply.totalEffect: The total effect is the product of the effects traversed:

deepSection.title: What if the function were \(e^{\sin(x^2)}\)?
deepSection.subtitle: The method does not change. We keep going inside until we reach x, collecting one factor per layer.

deepLayers.reading: The exponential remains exponential. Everything in the exponent stays fixed for now.
We enter the exponent: the sine becomes cosine, keeping x² as the argument.
We reach the last layer, the power, and differentiate it.

procedureBox.title: The procedure to reuse every time

procedure.title: Mentally circle the layers
procedure.text: Identify which function wraps all the others, then which are contained inside it.

procedure.title: Differentiate the outer layer
procedure.text: Leave everything inside its parentheses unchanged.

procedure.title: Enter one layer and multiply
procedure.text: Repeat: differentiate the new layer, keep what it contains, and add the factor to the product.

procedure.title: Stop when you reach x
procedure.text: At that point you have gone through all the layers; you can reorder and simplify the product.

derivation.howToRead: HOW TO READ IT AND WHEN TO USE IT
derivation.rereadAndRetry: Re-read the steps and try again.

fallingObject.title: An object is falling
fallingObject.body: Imagine watching a falling object. The distance it covers does not grow at a constant rate: every second it moves faster. From two positions we can compute the average velocity, but a speedometer shows something different: a velocity at that very instant.

observe.label: I OBSERVE
observe.body: The position at time t and shortly after, at time t + h.

measure.label: I MEASURE
measure.body: How much distance was covered during that small interval.

ask.label: I ASK
ask.body: We make the interval smaller and smaller, without setting it equal to zero.

bridge.title: The bridge to the limit
bridge.body1: Having posed the question, we can give it a language. If the position law is \(s(t)=\tfrac12gt^2\), the average velocity between \(t\) and \(t+h\) is:
bridge.body2: The instantaneous velocity emerges by observing what happens as \(h\) approaches zero. This is exactly the kind of question a limit answers.

historyNote.title: Galileo and the problem of velocity
historyNote.summary: Galileo describes accelerated motion in 1638, but he still lacks the calculus.
historyNote.body: Galileo understood that in free fall the distance grows as the square of time. He could describe motion over intervals, but he did not yet have a rigorous definition of instantaneous velocity. Newton and Leibniz would build the necessary tools some decades after his death.

alert.strong: Question to carry to the next section:
alert.body: if velocity is the slope of a position-time graph, how do we find the slope of a curve at a point?

guided.para1: Fix the point \(P=(x_0,f(x_0))\) and choose a second point \(Q=(x_0+h,f(x_0+h))\). The line through them is a secant.
guided.para2: As \(h\to0\), Q approaches P and the secant lines tend to a limiting position: the tangent line. Its slope is \(f'(x_0)\).

example.title: For f(x) = x² at x₀ = 1
example.step1: Substitute the function into the difference quotient.
example.step2: Expand the square and cancel h, which is non-zero while we compute the quotient.
example.step3: The slope of the tangent at x₀ = 1 is 2.

normal.title: The normal line
normal.para: The normal passes through the same point as the tangent but is perpendicular to it. If the tangent has a finite non-zero slope, \(m_n=-1/m_t\).
normal.note: If the tangent is horizontal, the normal is vertical: \(x=x_0\). If the tangent is vertical, the normal is horizontal: \(y=f(x_0)\).

historyNote.title: Leibniz, infinitesimals and dy/dx
historyNote.summary: The notation dy/dx preserves the geometric intuition of a ratio of changes.
historyNote.body: In 1675 Leibniz introduced the symbols dx and dy. He thought of them as infinitely small changes — a powerful idea, even though the rigorous foundation would come in the nineteenth century with Cauchy's definition of a limit.

box.heading: Definition
box.line1: f is said to be differentiable at x₀ if the following limit exists and is finite
box.line2: That number is the derivative of f at x₀.

atPoint.label: AT A POINT
atPoint.title: f′(x₀) is a number
atPoint.body: It measures the slope or rate of change at a specific point x₀.

asFunction.label: AT EVERY POINT
asFunction.title: f′(x) is a function
asFunction.body: By repeating the limit for every x we obtain a new function: the derivative function.

proof.title: The formula comes from the limit
proof.meaning: It states that the slope of the parabola \(y=x^2\), at every point \(x\), equals \(2x\). To the right of the origin it is positive, to the left it is negative, and at zero it is zero.

checkpoint.question: Why can we cancel the factor h?
checkpoint.choice0: Because in the quotient h is non-zero; the limit comes afterwards
checkpoint.explanation: Correct: we cancel for h≠0 and only then take the limit.

step3.label: Cancel h
step3.explanation: For \(h\neq0\) we can cancel the factor h.

step4.label: Take the limit
step4.explanation: As h tends to zero, \(2x\) remains.

historyNote.title: Newton and Leibniz: two languages for change
historyNote.summary: Two independent discoveries, a heated dispute and notations we still use today.
historyNote.body: Newton developed the method of fluxions by thinking of quantities that flow in time; Leibniz built a language of differentials better suited to symbolic computation. Today we use both intuitions, made rigorous by the theory of limits.

theorem.title: Differentiability ⇒ continuity
theorem.para: If f is differentiable at x₀, then it is continuous at x₀. The proof uses the same difference quotient:
theorem.note: Hence \(f(x_0+h)\to f(x_0)\). The converse fails: \(f(x)=|x|\) is continuous at 0 but the one-sided slopes are −1 and +1.

lab.title: What does the secant do at a singular point?
lab.para: Select the three cases and move x₀ to zero. At the corner the two one-sided slopes differ; at the cusp and the vertical tangent the slope does not remain finite.

corner.title: Corner point
corner.body: The one-sided derivatives exist and are finite, but have different values.

cusp.title: Cusp
cusp.body: The one-sided slopes become infinite with opposite signs: the graph forms a sharp point.

vertical.title: Vertical tangent
vertical.body: The slopes grow without bound with the same sign: the tangent is vertical.

geometric.label: GEOMETRIC
geometric.title: Slope of the tangent
geometric.body: On the graph, f′(x₀) gives how steeply the curve is inclined at the point x₀.

physical.label: PHYSICAL
physical.title: Instantaneous rate
physical.body: If f measures a quantity, f′ measures how rapidly it is changing.

velocity.title: Velocity
velocity.body: The derivative of position with respect to time.

current.title: Current
current.body: The rate at which electric charge flows.

growth.title: Growth
growth.body: The instantaneous growth rate of a population.

cost.title: Marginal cost
cost.body: How much it costs to produce one additional unit.

problem.title: How much does one extra unit cost?
problem.para: A small firm models its total cost, in euros, as \(C(q)=0{,}02q^2+8q+500\), where q is the number of units.
problem.interpretationBody: near 100 units, producing one additional unit increases the cost by about €12. The positive sign indicates an increase; the unit is euros per unit produced. The derivative enables a local decision without recalculating the entire cost.

closing.heading: Closing question
closing.question: "What is the derivative?"
closing.body: Try to answer without formulas, once as a geometer, once as an analyst, and once as a physicist. Then move on to worksheet §1.

historyNote.title: From orbits to machine learning
historyNote.summary: The derivative has become the common language of systems that change.
historyNote.body: From Newton's mechanics to the equations of electromagnetism, from marginal cost to the optimisation of machine-learning models, the derivative makes change into a computable object.

velocityInquiry.title: A small numerical experiment

lead.mid: . We want to estimate the velocity exactly at

velocityInquiry.predictionLabel: Before calculating: towards which velocity do you think we will converge?

result.post: and approach 20. The instantaneous velocity is therefore 20 units of space per unit of time.

warning.post: in the quotient: we would be dividing by zero. Instead, we compute the value the quotient approaches as h becomes small.

warmup.q1: What are the three readings of the derivative?
warmup.a1: Geometric: slope of the tangent. Analytic: limit of the difference quotient. Physical: instantaneous rate of change.
warmup.q2: What is the difference between f′(x₀) and f′(x)?
warmup.a2: f′(x₀) is a number attached to a specific point; f′(x) is the function that assigns to each x the slope at that point.
warmup.a3: No. |x| is continuous at zero but has one-sided derivatives −1 and +1, so it is not differentiable at zero.
warmup.objectiveHeading: Build the table — don't just receive it.
warmup.objectiveBody: Every fundamental formula and every rule will be derived from what we already know about limits.
warmup.prereqTitle: The two fundamental limits we will use
warmup.prereqBody: We are not proving them here: we recall them numerically and state them as known results. They are the necessary bridge for differentiating sine and the exponential without hidden steps.
warmup.limit1Note: For t = 0.1 the ratio is about 0.9983; for t = 0.01 it is about 0.99998.
warmup.limit2Note: For t = 0.1 the ratio is about 1.0517; for t = 0.01 it is about 1.0050.

fundamentals.powerMeaning: Used to differentiate a power of \(x\): the exponent \(n\) drops in front as a multiplier and then decreases by one. For example, \((x^3)'=3x^2\).
fundamentals.powerStep1: We start from the difference quotient.
fundamentals.powerStep2: The first term cancels \(x^n\); all others contain h.
fundamentals.powerStep3: After simplification only the first term carries no factor h.
fundamentals.powerStep4: Terms containing h tend to zero.
fundamentals.powerConclusion: The power rule is not a trick: it is the first coefficient of Newton's binomial that survives the limit.
fundamentals.sineMeaning: Cosine measures the slope of sine at the same point.
fundamentals.sineCheckQ: Which prerequisite makes the last step possible?
fundamentals.sineCheckExp: Correct: the standard limit recalled in the warm-up appears.
fundamentals.sineStep2: Prosthaphaeresis converts the difference into a product; find the term in the glossary.
fundamentals.sineStep3: The second factor tends to 1, as recalled in the warm-up.
fundamentals.cosineMeaning: States that the slope of cosine at \(x\) is the opposite of the value of sine at the same point. The minus sign indicates that cosine initially decreases.
fundamentals.cosineStep1: We substitute into the difference quotient.
fundamentals.cosineConclusion: Cosine differentiates to sine with a negative sign.
fundamentals.expInsightBody: It is the only function whose rate of growth always equals its own value. That is why it appears in bacterial growth, radioactive decay and continuous compound interest.
fundamentals.historySummary: When the rate of growth is proportional to the quantity present, eˣ appears.
fundamentals.historyBody: If a population grows at a rate proportional to its size, the equation is N′ = kN. Its solutions are exponential: the function eˣ is the natural model for processes with proportional feedback.

rules.linearityMeaning: Used for sums and multiples: \(f\) and \(g\) are functions, while \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are constant numbers. Each function is differentiated separately and the constants are kept.
rules.linearityStep1: We group the variations of f and g separately.
rules.linearityStep2: The limit of a sum is the sum of the limits; constants factor out.
rules.productMeaning: Used when \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) are multiplied. First differentiate \(f\) keeping \(g\) fixed, then keep \(f\) fixed and differentiate \(g\); finally add the two contributions.
rules.productCheckQ: Why does the formula contain two terms?
rules.productCheckC0: Each term measures the change in one factor while the other stays fixed
rules.productCheckC1: Because we simply multiply the two derivatives
rules.productCheckC2: Because a product always becomes a sum
rules.productCheckExp: Correct: the two terms separate the contributions of each factor.
rules.productStep1: The numerator cannot be separated directly.
rules.productStep2: We add and subtract \(f(x)g(x+h)\): this is Leibniz's trick.
rules.productStep3: We now recognise the two difference quotients.
rules.productConclusion: Differentiate one factor at a time, keeping the other fixed, then add the contributions.
rules.quotientMeaning: Used when a function \(f\) is divided by a function \(g\), with \(g(x)\neq0\). The order in the numerator matters: derivative of top times bottom, minus top times derivative of bottom.
rules.quotientStep1: We derive it from the product rule, with \(g\neq0\).
rules.quotientStep2: We apply the product rule to the right-hand side.
rules.quotientStep3: Move the second term to the left and divide by g.
rules.quotientConclusion: Order matters in the numerator: derivative of top times bottom minus top times derivative of bottom.
rules.chainMeaning: Used when one function is inside another: \(f\circ g\) means \(f(g(x))\). Differentiate the outer function evaluated at the inner, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
rules.chainStep1: The outer variation depends on the variation of the inner function.
rules.stepIntroduceK: Introduce k without dividing by zero
rules.chainStep2: Set φ(k)=[f(g(x)+k)-f(g(x))]/k for k≠0 and φ(0)=f′(g(x)). This keeps the identity valid even when the inner variation is zero.
rules.chainConclusion: Differentiate the outer function evaluated at the inner, then multiply by the derivative of the inner.
rules.afterChainTitle: Now we can justify the logarithm
rules.lnMeaning: The proof uses the chain rule, so it is presented only now.
rules.lnStep1: The logarithm is the inverse of the exponential.
rules.lnStep2: Differentiating e^y with respect to x yields dy/dx.
rules.lnConclusion: The proof is no longer circular: the chain rule has already been established.
rules.historyProductTitle: The trick in the product rule
rules.historyProductSummary: Adding and subtracting the same term transforms an opaque expression into two difference quotients.
rules.historyProductBody: The decisive step is inserting zero in the form f(x)g(x+h) − f(x)g(x+h). The value does not change, but it allows us to isolate the variation of each factor. This is a classic example of how a proof also suggests the best way to remember a formula.
rules.historyChainSummary: dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx is excellent intuition, but the limit explains why it works.
rules.historyChainBody: Leibniz's notation makes differentials look like fractions that cancel. The rigorous proof replaces this cancellation with two difference quotients and uses the continuity of the inner function.

secondDerivative.heading: Second derivative
secondDerivative.concaveUpBody: Slopes are increasing: the graph has the shape of a cup.
secondDerivative.concaveDownBody: Slopes are decreasing: the graph has the shape of a dome.
secondDerivative.lookFirstTitle: The second derivative is the direction in which the graph bends
secondDerivative.lookFirstBody: Remembering "cup" and "dome" is not enough. The second derivative compares the slopes of nearby tangents: if they increase, \(f''>0\); if they decrease, \(f''<0\). The yellow lines in the graphs make this variation visible.
secondDerivative.labTitle: Move the point and watch the curvature change
secondDerivative.labBody: Drag the point along the function and compare the tangent with the sign of \(f''\). If you open the detail panel, the
secondDerivative.labBodyEnd: adds information on how much and in which direction the curve is bending.
secondDerivative.stationaryBody: A point is stationary when \(f'(x_0)=0\): the tangent is horizontal. It may be a maximum, a minimum or an inflection point; to distinguish them we will need to study the sign of f′ and f″.
secondDerivative.stationaryNote: Both points have a horizontal tangent. The second derivative \(f''(x)=6x\) helps us determine that one is a maximum and the other a minimum.
secondDerivative.alert: This is only a bridge: the full analysis of maxima, minima and inflection points comes later. In the appendix after Taylor you will find Rolle, Lagrange and the other theorems read graphically and through practical cases.

taylor.advancedNote: This section is not part of the basic assessment.
taylor.beforeFormulaTitle: What are we trying to achieve?
taylor.beforeFormulaP1: Functions such as \(e^x\), \(\sin x\) or \(\cos x\) are not polynomials. Taylor constructs a local substitute, called the approximating polynomial: a formula made only of sums, products and powers, hence easy to compute and to graph.
taylor.beforeFormulaP2: "Approximating" does not mean finding an exact copy. It means choosing a point \(x_0\) and building a polynomial that shares the same value there and — by adding terms — the same slope, the same curvature and so on. Near \(x_0\) the two curves nearly overlap; farther away they may diverge.
taylor.card1Body: Use a simple polynomial in place of the original function, but only in the region where the resemblance is good enough.
taylor.card2Body: This is the point around which we build the approximation. Changing the centre means asking the polynomial to be accurate in a different region.
taylor.card3Body: At a point x it is the vertical distance between the two graphs: \(|f(x)-P_n(x)|\). A small error means a good approximation.
taylor.simpleExampleBody: Near zero, \(e^x\) resembles the line \(1+x\). For \(x=0.1\) we get \(1+0.1=1.1\), while the true value is about \(1.10517\). The error is about \(0.00517\): it is not zero, but we know exactly what we are losing by using the simpler formula.
taylor.buildTitle: How much information do we want to preserve?
taylor.step0Text: The constant polynomial knows only the height of the function at the chosen centre.
taylor.step1Text: We add the tangent line: at the centre the two curves also share the same direction.
taylor.step2Text: The second derivative makes the way the curve bends coincide as well.
taylor.summaryNote: You do not need to memorise the summation immediately: it simply says "take the information about the function at \(x_0\) and add it one piece at a time, from position to finer and finer variations".
taylor.labTitle: Move the centre and observe where the polynomial works
taylor.developsTitle: Three fundamental expansions centred at zero
taylor.macLaurinNote: When the centre is zero the expansion is also called a Maclaurin series. For these three functions the full series converges on all of ℝ, but with a finite number of terms the approximation is generally better near the centre.
taylor.insightBody: Every term uses a derivative of order k at the chosen centre. The derivative is the local DNA of the function: it contains information about value, direction, curvature and higher-order variations. The error, however, reminds us that local information does not mean equality everywhere.
taylor.historySummary: The formula was born in the eighteenth century; understanding when it truly represents the function took another century.
taylor.historyBody: Brook Taylor published the formula in 1715. Colin Maclaurin studied the case centred at zero systematically. In the nineteenth century Cauchy clarified that possessing derivatives of every order does not automatically guarantee that the series converges to the function.

taylorLab.dragHint: Drag to pan · scroll or buttons to zoom
taylorLab.canvasAriaLabel: Interactive graph of the function and its Taylor polynomial. Drag to pan and use the scroll wheel to zoom.

message.order0: We know only the value of the function at x₀ = {{x0}}.
message.order1: Value and slope now match: the polynomial is the tangent line.
message.order2: The second derivative adds curvature: the two curves agree over a longer range.
message.orderN: We use {{count}} local pieces of information: the value and derivatives up to order {{order}}.

polynomial.caption: DISPLAYED POLYNOMIAL
polynomial.roundingNote: Coefficients are rounded to three digits; the graph uses the full values.

taylorLab.errorLineNote: The green line measures the distance between the function and the polynomial at

challenge.title: Challenge: the minimum degree
challenge.instructions: Move the order slider and find the first degree for which the error at the green point is less than {{threshold}}.

feedback.noThresholdReached: None of the available orders reaches the threshold: move the point closer to the center.
feedback.exact: Correct: P{{order}} is the first polynomial that meets the threshold.

fermat.title: Fermat before the notation f′
fermat.summary: Fermat looked for maxima, minima and tangents with the method of adequality.
fermat.body: In the 1630s Pierre de Fermat developed an algebraic method for maxima, minima and tangents. He did not yet use limits or modern notation, but the idea anticipated the horizontal-tangent condition at smooth extrema.

rolleEtAl.title: Rolle, Lagrange and Cauchy
rolleEtAl.summary: A result on the roots of equations gave rise to the mean value theorem.
rolleEtAl.body: Michel Rolle published in 1691 the result now bearing his name, originally in the context of algebraic equations. Lagrange placed it within the new analysis; in the nineteenth century Cauchy gave the mean value theorem a rigorous formulation and proof.

darboux.title: Darboux and derivatives without jumps
darboux.summary: In 1875 Darboux proved that a derivative always takes intermediate values.
darboux.body: Gaston Darboux showed that a derivative can be discontinuous yet cannot jump directly from one slope to another. The result definitively separated two ideas: continuity and the intermediate value property.

lhopital.title: One rule, two names
lhopital.summary: L'Hôpital's rule appeared in the first calculus textbook, but came from Johann Bernoulli's lectures.
lhopital.body: In 1696 Guillaume de l'Hôpital published Analyse des infiniment petits, the first systematic calculus textbook. The rule bears his name, but historical documents show the result came from Johann Bernoulli's lectures, which l'Hôpital had sponsored.

taylorError.title: Lagrange, Cauchy and the Taylor remainder
taylorError.summary: The remainder turns a good approximation into a controllable estimate.
taylorError.body: Lagrange formulated one of the most widely used expressions for the Taylor remainder; Cauchy developed another form and helped clarify the convergence hypotheses. The practical idea is modern and decisive: approximating is not enough — one must know how large the error can be.

fermat.title: Fermat's Theorem
fermat.subtitle: Where to look for maxima and minima
fermat.hypotheses: The point \(x_0\) is interior to the domain, the function is differentiable at \(x_0\), and has a local maximum or minimum there.
fermat.geometry: At a smooth extremum the curve cannot keep rising or falling: the tangent must be horizontal.
fermat.use: Reduces the search for extrema to stationary points and points where the derivative does not exist.
fermat.caution: This is a necessary condition, not sufficient: \(f(x)=x^3\) has \(f^{\prime}(0)=0\), but zero is not an extremum.

rolle.title: Rolle's Theorem
rolle.subtitle: Same height, horizontal tangent
rolle.hypotheses: \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and takes the same value at both endpoints.
rolle.geometry: If the path starts and ends at the same height, at least one intermediate point has a horizontal tangent.
rolle.use: Allows counting or separating zeros: between two distinct zeros of \(f\) there is at least one zero of \(f^{\prime}\).
rolle.caution: It guarantees the existence of at least one point, but says nothing about where it is or whether it is unique.

lagrange.title: Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem
lagrange.subtitle: An instantaneous rate equals the average rate
lagrange.hypotheses: \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([a,b]\) and differentiable on its interior.
lagrange.geometry: There exists at least one tangent line parallel to the chord joining the two endpoints of the graph.
lagrange.use: Links total variation and instantaneous rate; also allows estimating how much a function can change.
lagrange.caution: The theorem guarantees \(c\), but generally provides no formula for computing it.

monotone.title: Monotonicity Test
monotone.subtitle: The sign of the derivative orients the graph
monotone.hypotheses: \(f\) is continuous on the interval and differentiable on its interior; the sign of \(f^{\prime}\) is checked over the entire interval.
monotone.geometry: Tangents with positive slope accompany a rising graph; negative slopes accompany a falling graph.
monotone.use: Allows comparing function values without computing all of them, and reading local behaviour.
monotone.caution: An isolated zero of \(f^{\prime}\) does not necessarily interrupt monotonicity: \(x^3\) remains increasing through zero.

secondTest.title: Second Derivative Test
secondTest.subtitle: Classifying a stationary point
secondTest.hypotheses: The function is twice differentiable near \(x_0\) and \(f^{\prime}(x_0)=0\).
secondTest.geometry: A horizontal tangent inside a cup identifies a minimum; inside a cap it identifies a maximum.
secondTest.use: Quickly classifies many stationary points without constructing a full sign chart for \(f^{\prime}\).
secondTest.caution: If \(f^{\prime\prime}(x_0)=0\), the test is inconclusive: \(x^4\), \(-x^4\) and \(x^3\) yield three different behaviours.

convexity.title: Convexity Test
convexity.subtitle: The sign of f″ describes curvature
convexity.hypotheses: The second derivative exists on the interval and maintains the same sign throughout.
convexity.geometry: When \(f^{\prime\prime}>0\) the tangents lie below the graph; when \(f^{\prime\prime}<0\) they lie above.
convexity.use: Allows understanding which way the curve bends and identifying possible inflection points.
convexity.caution: The single value \(f^{\prime\prime}(x_0)=0\) is not enough to assert that \(x_0\) is an inflection point: a change of concavity is required.

cauchy.title: Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem
cauchy.subtitle: Two variations compared at the same point
cauchy.hypotheses: \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and \(g^{\prime}\neq0\).
cauchy.geometry: The parametric curve \((g(t),f(t))\) has a tangent parallel to the chord between the endpoints.
cauchy.use: Compares two quantities changing together and is the theoretical basis for L'Hôpital's rule.
cauchy.caution: The hypotheses must be checked for both functions, and the denominator of the ratio must be meaningful.

darboux.title: Darboux's Theorem
darboux.subtitle: Slopes cannot jump
darboux.hypotheses: \(f\) is differentiable on an interval; the derivative function need not be assumed continuous.
darboux.geometry: As the tangent rotates from one slope to another, it passes through every intermediate inclination.
darboux.use: Allows ruling out that a step function is the derivative of any function.
darboux.caution: Having all intermediate values does not mean being continuous: a derivative can be discontinuous without making jumps.

lhopital.title: L'Hôpital's Rule
lhopital.subtitle: Comparing rates of vanishing or growth
lhopital.hypotheses: The ratio has an indeterminate form \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\), the functions are differentiable near the point, and the limit of the ratio of derivatives exists.
lhopital.geometry: Near the common point, the ratio of heights is replaced by the ratio of slopes.
lhopital.use: Simplifies limits such as \(\lim_{x\to0}\sin x/x\) or comparisons between exponential and polynomial growth.
lhopital.caution: It does not apply to every fraction: the indeterminate form must be verified first, and the procedure sometimes needs to be repeated.

inverse.title: Derivative of the Inverse Function
inverse.subtitle: Reflecting the graph swaps the slopes
inverse.geometry: The graphs of \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) are symmetric about \(y=x\); the slopes of the tangents are reciprocals.
inverse.use: Derives naturally the derivatives of logarithm, square root and inverse trigonometric functions.
inverse.caution: If \(f^{\prime}(x_0)=0\), the inverse may have a vertical tangent and the formula yields no finite value.

taylorError.title: Taylor's Theorem with Lagrange Remainder
taylorError.subtitle: Measuring the error of the approximation
taylorError.hypotheses: \(f\) possesses the necessary derivatives between the centre \(a\) and the point \(x\).
taylorError.geometry: The polynomial agrees locally with the value and derivatives; the remainder measures the vertical distance still visible from the curve.
taylorError.use: Establishes how many digits or what precision we can expect from a Taylor approximation.
taylorError.caution: The error depends on a higher-order derivative at an unknown point \(\xi\): it must be estimated over the whole interval.

prediction.question: Before revealing: as we approach from the left and from the right, will the slopes tend to the same value?
prediction.feedbackClose: The two slopes are now very close: the two-sided limit is consistent with a derivative. h never becomes zero: the ratio would be undefined.
prediction.feedbackFar: The one-sided slopes do not coincide yet. Reduce |h|; if they remain different, the derivative does not exist. h never becomes zero: the ratio would be undefined.
